about: Sourced life stories for prophets-north: Micaiah son of Imlah, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah and Jonah son of Amittai. Written from Scripture and the dossier Research/People/prophets-north.md. Elijah's and Elisha's stories are written elsewhere.

micaiah-1ki-22-8.short: Micaiah son of Imlah, the prophet of the LORD whom Ahab said he hated, foretold Israel scattered before Ramoth-gilead and was sent to prison.

paragraphs.text: Micaiah son of Imlah appears in one scene, told in 1 Kings 22 and again, almost word for word, in 2 Chronicles 18, which spells his father's name Imla. Jehoshaphat king of Judah had come down to Ahab king of Israel, and they planned to take Ramoth-gilead from Syria. The king gathered about four hundred prophets, who all said, “Go up”. Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there not here a prophet of the LORD besides, that we might enquire of him?” The king of Israel named Micaiah, “but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.”

The messenger sent to fetch him urged him to speak good like the rest. Micaiah answered, “As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.” Before the two kings at the gate of Samaria his first answer echoed the others, until the king adjured him to tell nothing but the truth. Then he said he had seen all Israel scattered upon the hills “as sheep that have not a shepherd”, and the LORD on his throne, with a spirit sent to be “a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets”.

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah struck him on the cheek, and Micaiah answered, “Behold, thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself.” The king ordered him taken back to Amon the governor of the city and Joash the king's son, to be fed with “bread of affliction and with water of affliction” until the king came in peace. Micaiah's last recorded words were, “If thou return at all in peace, the LORD hath not spoken by me,” and “Hearken, O people, every one of you.” The king went up to Ramoth-gilead in disguise, was struck by an arrow and died at even. Scripture does not say what became of Micaiah.

zedekiah-1ki-22-11.short: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah, one of Ahab's four hundred prophets, made horns of iron, promised victory over Syria and struck Micaiah on the cheek.

paragraphs.text: Scripture says little of Zedekiah son of Chenaanah: he appears only in the scene before Ramoth-gilead, told in 1 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 18. When Ahab king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah sat on their thrones at the gate of Samaria and the prophets prophesied before them, Zedekiah “made him horns of iron” and said, “Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them.” All the prophets said the same: “Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and prosper”.

Micaiah then told the kings that the LORD had put “a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets”. Zedekiah came near, struck Micaiah on the cheek and asked, “Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?” Micaiah answered, “Behold, thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself.” Scripture does not mention Zedekiah again; it tells that the king went up to Ramoth-gilead, was struck by an arrow in the battle and died.

jonah-2ki-14-25.short: Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher, foretold Israel's restored borders, fled from the LORD's call to Nineveh, was swallowed by a great fish, and then preached there.

paragraphs.text: Jonah was the son of Amittai, a prophet of Gath-hepher. Kings says that Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel “restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah”. The words of that prophecy are not recorded.

The book that bears his name begins, “Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai”, sending him to cry against Nineveh, “that great city”. Instead he went down to Joppa and took ship for Tarshish, “from the presence of the LORD”. In a great storm the mariners cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. He told them he was an Hebrew who feared the LORD, and that they should cast him into the sea. They rowed hard, prayed to the LORD, and cast him in, “and the sea ceased from her raging”.

“The LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah”, and he was in its belly three days and three nights. He prayed there, ending, “Salvation is of the LORD”, and at the LORD's word the fish vomited him out upon the dry land.

The word came to him the second time, and he went to Nineveh and cried, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” The people believed God and fasted in sackcloth, and the king of Nineveh, whom the book does not name, sat in ashes and called all to turn from their evil way. Then “God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.”

This displeased Jonah. He said it was why he had fled, “for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful”, and asked to die. He made a booth on the east side of the city to see what would become of it; the LORD God prepared a gourd to shade him, then a worm that smote it so that it withered, and a vehement east wind. The book ends with the LORD's question: should he not spare Nineveh, with more than sixscore thousand persons who could not discern their right hand from their left, “and also much cattle?” Scripture tells nothing of Jonah after this.

Jesus spoke of “the sign of the prophet Jonas”: “as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.” He said that the men of Nineveh “repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here.”
